Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling during the past seven days, designed to help us spot any symptoms of depression or anxiety that can creep up after baby arrives.  

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team; we want you to feel completely safe and heard. After we finish, we’ll talk about what the score means and, if needed, map out next steps for extra support.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can start with the first question:

Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?
Oh—yeah, I’ve still been laughing. My husband did that silly dance with the burp cloth last night and I totally cracked up. So, no, laughing hasn’t felt hard.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, definitely—I’ve still been laughing.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I still look forward to stuff. Like, I’m excited for our family walk to the coffee truck this weekend—baby’s first outing. So, yeah, enjoyment is still there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. If the baby spits up a ton or won’t settle, I figure it’s just part of the newborn deal, not something I did wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit, maybe. Sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing is okay or if that tiny cough means something bad, even though there’s no real reason to think it. It’s not constant, just pops up out of nowhere once or twice a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt scared or panicky—just those quick worries about the baby, nothing that feels like panic.
Things have been getting on top of me
Not really. Sure, I’m tired and there’s a lot to juggle, but most days I feel like I’m keeping up okay.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No—once I finally lie down, I sleep pretty well. I’m tired, but not upset enough to keep me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt sad or miserable—just a little tired and sometimes worried, but overall I’m okay.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried at all this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never—hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind.

You're doing beautifully in these early weeks of motherhood, still finding joy in small moments like your husband's silly burp-cloth dance and eagerly planning baby's first outing to the coffee truck. While you admit to the occasional <sym>worry spike</sym> about your little one's breathing, you're sleeping when you can, not feeling overwhelmed, and you've had no sad or hopeless spells.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 2, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient reports sudden, unprovoked worries about the baby occurring once or twice daily, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your score of 2 falls well below the threshold where <med>postpartum depression</med> is probable. You endorse only one item (Q4) at the mild level, describing isolated, baby-focused <sym>worries</sym> without pervasive low mood, hopelessness, sleep-mood linkage, or self-harm ideation, which do not meet <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine postpartum visits with your midwife or <med>obstetrician</med>
2. Re-take the EPDS if mood, anxiety, sleep, or coping worsen
3. Share any escalating worries or new physical symptoms with your <med>primary care provider</med>
4. Keep leaning on your support system and schedule small enjoyable activities for yourself
5. Practice brief breathing or grounding exercises when a worry spike hits
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 2: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening (Edinburgh Scale)

Positive endorsements  
• Enjoyment/humor intact (items 1, 2)  
• No excessive self-blame, crying spells, sleep-mood link, or self-harm ideation (items 3, 7, 9, 10)

Areas of note  
• Mild, situational worries about infant well-being, 1–2×/day, without panic or persistent apprehension (items 4, 5)  
• Denies pervasive sadness, hopelessness, or feeling overwhelmed (items 6, 8)

Screening summary  
Patient reports isolated, baby-focused worries; no current evidence of significant depressive or anxiety symptoms. No safety concerns identified. Continue routine postpartum follow-up and education on perinatal mood changes; re-screen if distress escalates or new symptoms emerge.
